title: loki helm upgrade failed from helm version 2.11.1 to 3.3.3 on eks 1.24 version
body:
### What happened?

Hi Team I will be updating eks version 1.25 for that need to upgrade loki helm chart as pod security policy is getting depricated. but getting me below error. We have ovverrided some of the values.yaml configuration as well

Error: execution error at (loki/templates/validate.yaml:2:4): Top level 'config' is not allowed. Most common configuration sections are exposed under the loki section. If you need to override the whole config, provide the configuration as a string that can contain template expressions under loki.config. Alternatively, you can provide the configuration as an external secret.
│
│ with module.service.helm_release.loki,
│ on ........\modules\loki\helm.tf line 1, in resource "helm_release" "loki":
│ 1: resource "helm_release" "loki" {

### What did you expect to happen?

I want to upgrade the loki helm chart as pod security policy is getting depricated on EKS version 1.25

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

installed loki helm chart on EKS version 1.24 currently 

### Anything else we need to know?

overridedn yaml files: loki_config.yaml

title: HA Cluster initialization issues
body:
### What happened?

During the initialization of the very first control-plane-nodes (3 control-plane-nodes + 3 worker-nodes) I'm getting these errors : 

    root@k8s-eu-1-control-plane-node-1:~# sudo kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint k82-eu-1-load-balancer-dns-1:53 --upload-certs --v=8 --ignore-preflight-errors=Port-6443

    
    Unfortunately, an error has occurred:
	    timed out waiting for the condition
    
    This error is likely caused by:
	    - The kubelet is not running
	    - The kubelet is unhealthy due to a misconfiguration of the node in some way (required cgroups disabled)
    
    If you are on a systemd-powered system, you can try to troubleshoot the error with the following commands:
	    - 'systemctl status kubelet'
	    - 'journalctl -xeu kubelet'
    
    Additionally, a control plane component may have crashed or exited when started by the container runtime.
    To troubleshoot, list all containers using your preferred container runtimes CLI.
    Here is one example how you may list all running Kubernetes containers by using crictl:
	    - 'crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///var/run/containerd/containerd.sock ps -a | grep kube | grep -v pause'
	    Once you have found the failing container, you can inspect its logs with:
	    - 'crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///var/run/containerd/containerd.sock logs CONTAINERID'


This is the complete output of the failed initialization :

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iEnu34unu7xnsh556eTbY5EAJ-2zBrkr/view?usp=sharing

Output of `journalctl -xeu kubelet` : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1d_Z6ic2xjyXu1QIpdba655yS4bvcfhkl/view?usp=drive_link

    root@k8s-eu-1-control-plane-node-1:~# 
    root@k8s-eu-1-control-plane-node-1:~# crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///var/run/containerd/containerd.sock logs 579c2b9e5d17a

      33348 pts/0    R+     0:00 grep --color=auto 6443

Initialization process OK

Based on what is described here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/blob/main/docs/ha-considerations.md#keepalived-configuration

I defined:

title: Unable to install/init kubernetes>1.23.17 on centos9stream (on kcli vm)
body:
### What happened?

I'm using `kcli` to create a kube. Everything works well on ubuntu and centos8stream, but the `kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "${API_IP}:6443" --pod-network-cidr $CIDR --certificate-key $CERTKEY --upload-certs --token $TOKEN --token-ttl 0 -v 5 --kubernetes-version=$VERSION` fails when using centos9stream with kubernetes>1.23.17.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `kubeadm init` should succeed

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
kcli create kube generic -P domain="example.com" -P pool=default -P ctlplanes=1 -P workers=1 -P network=default -P image=centos9stream -P sdn=flannel -P nfs=false -P disk_size=40 mycluster
```

Alternatively get a centos9stream VM with enough memory and disk size and run:

```
export PATH=/root:$PATH
test -f /etc/profile.d/kcli.sh && source /etc/profile.d/kcli.sh
echo """[kubernetes]
name=Kubernetes
baseurl=https://packages.cloud.google.com/yum/repos/kubernetes-el7-x86_64
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0
repo_gpgcheck=0""" >/etc/yum.repos.d/kubernetes.repo
echo net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf
modprobe br_netfilter
sysctl -p
setenforce 0
sed -i "s/SELINUX=enforcing/SELINUX=permissive/" /etc/selinux/config
VERSION=$(dnf --showduplicates list kubectl  | grep kubectl | tail -1 | awk '{print $2}' | xargs)

TARGET=centos
[ "$TARGET" == 'fedora' ] && dnf -y remove zram-generator-defaults && swapoff -a
modprobe overlay
modprobe br_netfilter
cat <<EOF | tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-cri.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward                 = 1
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
EOF
sysctl --system
dnf install -y yum-utils device-mapper-persistent-data lvm2
yum-config-manager --add-repo https://download.docker.com/linux/$TARGET/docker-ce.repo
dnf install -y containerd.io
mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml
[ "$TARGET" == 'fedora' ] && sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = .*/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml
systemctl enable --now containerd
systemctl restart containerd

dnf -y install -y kubelet-$VERSION kubectl-$VERSION kubeadm-$VERSION git openssl
systemctl enable --now kubelet
PKGMGR="dnf"
$PKGMGR -y install keepalived
NETMASK=$(ip -o -f inet addr show | awk '/scope global/ {print $4}' | head -1 | cut -d'/' -f2)
sed -i "s/NETMASK/$NETMASK/" /root/keepalived.conf
NIC=$(find /sys/class/net -type l -not -lname '*virtual*' -printf '%f\n' | head -1)
sed -i "s/NIC/$NIC/" /root/keepalived.conf
cp /root/keepalived.conf /etc/keepalived
systemctl enable --now keepalived
#!/usr/bin/bash

# set global variable
CIDR="10.244.0.0/16"

API_IP=192.168.122.253

DOMAIN=kata.com

# initialize cluster
CERTKEY=95c996e0072baf4b995610fda130d4837debfd12de0470358bf8a4ea5bdd36a8
TOKEN=rlj9fn.t1xf03l1alcmb6n7
kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "${API_IP}:6443" --pod-network-cidr $CIDR --certificate-key $CERTKEY --upload-certs --token $TOKEN --token-ttl 0

# config cluster credentials
cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf /root/kubeconfig
chown root:root /root/kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=/root/kubeconfig
echo "export KUBECONFIG=/root/kubeconfig" >> /root/.bashrc


# install Container Network Interface (CNI)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flannel-io/flannel/master/Documentation/kube-flannel.yml

# config cluster credentials
mkdir -p /root/.kube
cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf /root/.kube/config
chown root:root /root/.kube/config

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/k8snetworkplumbingwg/multus-cni/master/deployments/multus-daemonset-thick.yml
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I have tested 1.23.17,1.24.0,1.24.1,1.24.2,1.24.3,1.24.4,1.24.5,1.24.6,1.24.7,1.24.8,1.24.9,1.24.10,1.24.11,1.24.12,1.24.13,1.24.14,1.24.15,1.24.16,1.24.17,1.25.0,1.25.1,1.25.2,1.25.3,1.25.4,1.25.5,1.25.6,1.25.7,1.25.8,1.25.9,1.25.10,1.25.11,1.25.12,1.25.13,1.25.14,1.26.9,1.27.6,1.28.0,1.28.2 versions by running a custom `check.sh` script using the version as first argument:

```
#!/bin/bash
CIDR="10.244.0.0/16"
API_IP=192.168.122.253
DOMAIN=kata.com
# initialize cluster
CERTKEY=95c996e0072baf4b995610fda130d4837debfd12de0470358bf8a4ea5bdd36a8
TOKEN=rlj9fn.t1xf03l1alcmb6n7
VERSION="$1"
dnf install -y kubelet-$VERSION-0 kubectl-$VERSION-0 kubeadm-$VERSION-0 git openssl
systemctl restart kubelet
kubeadm reset --force
kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "${API_IP}:6443" --pod-network-cidr $CIDR --certificate-key $CERTKEY --upload-certs --token $TOKEN --token-ttl 0 -v 5 --kubernetes-version=$VERSION
```

title: api-server tracing feature breaks port-forwarding - v1.25.10
body:
### What happened?

When we enabled the tracing feature for api-server, we noticed that port-forwarding was not working properly. All port-forwarding connections are getting timeout. 

[v1-25 Ref Doc](https://v1-25.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-traces/)

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that port forwarding should not be affected by enabling tracing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

<details>

* provision a k8s cluster with v1.25.10 version
* observe port-forwarding works fine before tracing
* enable tracing for api-server
* observe port-forwarding is broken

</details>

### Anything else we need to know?

Api-server configuration
<details>

```yaml

kind: Pod
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubeadm.kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver.advertise-address.endpoint: 192.168.64.43:6443
  creationTimestamp: null

    component: kube-apiserver
    tier: control-plane
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:

    - --enable-bootstrap-token-auth=true
```

title: Pod ready condition is updated to True after readiness gates condition is False
body:
### What happened?

I have a Deployment with 3 replicas. It have deafined custom readinessGates condition. But sometimes after readinessGates condition gets changed to False, pod ready condition still set to True.
pod Status:
```yaml
status:
  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-11-22T11:31:51Z"
    status: "False"
    type: custom-readiness-gate
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-11-22T11:31:49Z"
    status: "True"
    type: Initialized
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-11-22T11:31:59Z"
    status: "True"
    type: Ready
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-11-22T11:31:59Z"
    status: "True"
    type: ContainersReady
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-11-22T11:31:49Z"
    status: "True"
    type: PodScheduled
```
describe pod:
```yaml
Conditions:
  Type                             Status
  custom-readiness-gate            False
  Initialized                      True
  Ready                            True
  ContainersReady                  True
  PodScheduled                     True
```

### What did you expect to happen?

pod condition type==ready status should be updated to True with all conditions True. If the custom readiness-gates condition is False, the Ready condition can no be True.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

create a Deployment with 3 replicas, and update it, sometime will reproduce

### Anything else we need to know?

we should notice that the custom readinessGates condition is set at `2023-11-22T11:31:51Z`, but the Ready condition is set at `2023-11-22T11:31:59Z`, but it still changes to True although custom readinessGates condition is False

title: Kube-proxy not creating iptables rules on 1.28
body:
### What happened?

We created an EKS cluster on 1.28 using kube-proxy in iptables mode, and a majority of nodes fail to become ready.  Kube-proxy is running and not restarting.  On inspection we noticed that kube-proxy logs do not contain errors but looking at iptables (`iptables -t nat -L`) there appear to be no KUBE-SVC chains created.  Some nodes start fine and we see lots of iptables rules configured as expected.



### What did you expect to happen?

KUBE-SVC rules to be created so that networking is functional.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We consistently see this when creating a cluster and adding nodes.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Running conformance test on 1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster with sonobuoy fails
body:
### What happened?

@rtheis reported that conformance testing with the latest version of sonobuoy against a version 1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster fails on the support the 1.17 Sample API Server using the current Aggregator test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283#issuecomment-1812399851, related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283.

I found the reason why the test is working fine in Kubernetes CI jobs but fails with sonobuoy is because **the service account used by sonobuoy "sonobuoy-serviceaccount" doesn't have read permission of the non-resource url "/"**, which is used by the test to confirm the removal of group path:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec5096fa869b801d6eb1bf019819287ca61edc4d/test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go#L744-L746

```
I1121 14:31:40.149085       1 rbac.go:119] RBAC: no rules authorize user "system:serviceaccount:sonobuoy:sonobuoy-serviceaccount" with groups ["system:serviceaccounts" "system:serviceaccounts:son
thenticated"] to "get" nonResourceURL "/" cluster-wide
I1121 14:31:40.149099       1 authorization.go:87] "Forbidden" URI="/" reason=""
I1121 14:31:40.149218       1 httplog.go:132] "HTTP" verb="GET" URI="/" latency="327.429µs" userAgent="e2e.test/v1.29.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/1f69e12 -- [sig-api-machinery] Aggregator Should b
 the 1.17 Sample API Server using the current Aggregator [Conformance]" audit-ID="46c27282-7af6-48d1-bf3e-ca439c57bc92" srcIP="172.18.0.4:36878" apf_pl="workload-low" apf_fs="service-accounts" ap
eats=0 apf_additionalLatency="0s" apf_execution_time="105.94µs" resp=403
```

The permission of "sonobuoy-serviceaccount" is as below:
https://github.com/vmware-tanzu/sonobuoy/blob/6f9e27f1795f10475c9f6f5decdff692e1e228da/pkg/client/gen.go#L502-L505
```
cr.Rules = []v1.PolicyRule{
	{
		APIGroups: []string{"*"},
		Resources: []string{"*"},
		Verbs:     []string{"*"},
	},
	{
		NonResourceURLs: []string{"/metrics", "/logs", "/logs/*"},
		Verbs:           []string{"get"},
	},
}
```

There may be two ways to fix it:
1. Update the RBAC rule of sonobuoy to include "get" of "/". However, could other test runners encounter this issue? Is there a doc listing the required permissions for running e2e tests?
2. Update the e2e to skip checking the removal of the group path if the service account doesn't have permission to access the root path.

Which way do we usually prefer? 


### What did you expect to happen?

Running e2e with sonobuoy should succeed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a v1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster.
2. Run `sonobuoy run --e2e-focus "Sample API Server using the current Aggregator"`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

question here is what are the set of client permissions required to run the conformance suite?
perhaps a `cluster-admin`  level of access or a more granular recommendation should be documented.

@sttts what is your take on the root path requirement as approver for:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283/files#diff-d9472590663e3c095a5e1f62d1483eb7cda4f61fc725daebb0934db5f5bccdd8R744-R746

i wanted to PR the admin note in our conformance docs under sig-arch, but then i saw this:
https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/conformance-tests.md

> it is non-privileged (e.g., does not require root on nodes, access to raw network interfaces, or cluster admin permissions)

so https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283 broke this guarantee.
sounds like SIG Arch needs to comment.

> so https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283 broke this guarantee.

This statement surprises me. Root discovery is one of the least-privileged permissions you can have on a cluster. For years this was even open for unauthorized users on the internet (if your api endpoint has been exposed).

In other words, just add the `/` permission. While thinking about it, it is surprising that the user in question does not have this access already. Don't we allow that for every authorized user?

In contrast, I hope that lots of privileged operations are tested by conformance today. If we don't test things like admission webhooks for example, we have much bigger problems. And admission webhooks are basically equivalent to cluster-admin.

```
volumeMounts:

  - hostPath:

    name: k8s-certs
```
Then I realized kube-apiserver's args with file must read path only from one of `volumeMounts.mountPath[*]`,  so i updated my args:

```
spec:
```

title: DNS-1035 validation mismatch
body:
### What happened?

When creating a `Service` with a name that starts with a digit, Kubernetes return this error:

 
> Service "94924f13c1c1d259-d98b37350debffcf" is invalid: metadata.name: Invalid value: "94924f13c1c1d259-d98b37350debffcf": a DNS-1035 label must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters or '-', start with an alphabetic character, and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'my-name',  or 'abc-123', regex used for validation is '\[a-z\]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?')


### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that you could create a `Service` with a name that starts with a digit, as the error states:

```
a DNS-1035 label [...] start with an alphabetic character, and end with an alphanumeric character
```

But the regex shown in the message doesn't match the error description:
```
 '[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?')
```
should be
```
 '[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?')
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this resource to k8s

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: 001-service
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
```

title: CVE-2023-5528: Insufficient input sanitization in in-tree storage plugin leads to privilege escalation on Windows nodes
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) - **HIGH** (7.2)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where a user that can create pods and persistent volumes on Windows nodes may be able to escalate to admin privileges on those nodes. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if they are using an in-tree storage plugin for Windows nodes.

### Am I vulnerable?

Any kubernetes environment with Windows nodes is impacted.  Run `kubectl get nodes -l kubernetes.io/os=windows` to see if any Windows nodes are in use.

#### Affected Versions

- kubelet >= v1.8.0 (including all later minor versions)

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

The provided patch fully mitigates the vulnerability.

Outside of applying the provided patch, there are no known mitigations to this vulnerability.

#### Fixed Versions

- kubelet master - fixed by #121881
- kubelet v1.28.4 - fixed by #121882
- kubelet v1.27.8 - fixed by #121883
- kubelet v1.26.11 - fixed by #121884
- kubelet v1.25.16 - fixed by #121885

To upgrade, refer to the documentation:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/cluster-management/#upgrading-a-cluster

### Detection

Kubernetes audit logs can be used to detect if this vulnerability is being exploited. Persistent Volume create events with local path fields containing special characters are a strong indication of exploitation.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

This vulnerability was reported by Tomer Peled [@tomerpeled92](https://github.com/tomerpeled92)

title: Kubernetes 1.26.1: Unexplained Authentication Error, Unexpected Resolution, and Certificate Renewal Quandaries
body:
### What happened?

We encountered an issue where kubectl commands were failing with authentication-related errors, specifically mentioning the inability to get the current server API group list and a request for the client to provide credentials

For example:

kubectl get ns

returned:

E1108 17:25:17.087455 1494015 memcache.go:238] couldn't get current server API group list: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials
E1108 17:25:17.089374 1494015 memcache.go:238] couldn't get current server API group list: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials
E1108 17:25:17.091456 1494015 memcache.go:238] couldn't get current server API group list: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials
E1108 17:25:17.093366 1494015 memcache.go:238] couldn't get current server API group list: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials
E1108 17:25:17.095556 1494015 memcache.go:238] couldn't get current server API group list: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)


It happend in multiple clusters that were created at the same day a year ago.
During the troubleshooting process, we executed sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration to inspect the expiration status of certificates in the cluster. The output revealed the expiration dates of various certificates, including those used by the control plane components, and confirmed that the Certificate Authorities (CA) had ample time before expiration.

sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration

returned:

[check-expiration] Reading configuration from the cluster...
[check-expiration] FYI: You can look at this config file with 'kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml'

CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
admin.conf                 Mar 28, 2024 14:23 UTC   140d            ca                      no
apiserver                  Mar 28, 2024 14:22 UTC   140d            ca                      no
apiserver-etcd-client      Mar 28, 2024 14:22 UTC   140d            etcd-ca                 no
apiserver-kubelet-client   Mar 28, 2024 14:22 UTC   140d            ca                      no
controller-manager.conf    Mar 28, 2024 14:22 UTC   140d            ca                      no
etcd-healthcheck-client    Mar 28, 2024 13:45 UTC   140d            etcd-ca                 no
etcd-peer                  Mar 28, 2024 13:45 UTC   140d            etcd-ca                 no
etcd-server                Mar 28, 2024 13:45 UTC   140d            etcd-ca                 no
front-proxy-client         Mar 28, 2024 14:22 UTC   140d            front-proxy-ca          no
scheduler.conf             Mar 28, 2024 14:23 UTC   140d            ca                      no

CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
ca                      Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no
etcd-ca                 Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no
front-proxy-ca          Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no




But we also found that:

sudo openssl x509 -noout -dates -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt

returned:

notBefore=Nov  8 13:56:46 2022 GMT
notAfter=Nov  8 13:56:46 2023 GMT

However, when we manually renewed this certificate the issue persisted, and kubectl commands continued to face authentication errors.

This raised questions about the automatic renewal process, as we expected the kubelet certificate to be renewed automatically by the Kubernetes system. Despite having other certificates successfully renewed through manual intervention, the kubelet certificate renewal, which we understood should occur automatically, did not happen. This discrepancy added complexity to the troubleshooting process, leading us to investigate why the expected automatic renewal of the kubelet certificate did not take place. Clarifying this aspect is crucial for understanding the root cause and ensuring the expected behavior of the Kubernetes certificate management system.

The resolution, though its effectiveness remains unclear, involved executing the command sudo kubeadm certs renew all. This command successfully renewed all non-expired certificates, extending their expiration dates. Notably, it did not alter the /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt, which continued to be expired. Despite the kubelet certificate retaining its expired status, the execution of kubectl commands was restored to normal functionality following this renewal process. The reason behind this unexpected behavior, where the renewal of other certificates impacted kubectl even when the kubelet certificate remained expired, remains a point of inquiry.

We did:

sudo kubeadm certs renew all
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration

And got:

[check-expiration] Reading configuration from the cluster...
[check-expiration] FYI: You can look at this config file with 'kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml'

CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
admin.conf                 Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            ca                      no
apiserver                  Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            ca                      no
apiserver-etcd-client      Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            etcd-ca                 no
apiserver-kubelet-client   Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            ca                      no
controller-manager.conf    Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            ca                      no
etcd-healthcheck-client    Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            etcd-ca                 no
etcd-peer                  Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            etcd-ca                 no
etcd-server                Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            etcd-ca                 no
front-proxy-client         Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            front-proxy-ca          no
scheduler.conf             Nov 08, 2024 13:38 UTC   364d            ca                      no

CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY   EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
ca                      Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no
etcd-ca                 Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no
front-proxy-ca          Nov 05, 2032 14:55 UTC   8y              no



We're left with several questions after this experience. First, why did the initial error happen? Second, why did using sudo kubeadm certs renew all fix the problem, even though the kubelet certificate stayed expired? Third, why did renewing non-expired certificates make a difference? We also want to know the best practices for solving this kind of issue and why the automatic renewal, expected in Kubernetes 1.15 and later, didn't happen. These questions highlight the need for a clearer understanding of what occurred and guidance on managing certificates effectively in Kubernetes clusters.








### What did you expect to happen?

We expected that the Kubernetes cluster, running version 1.26.1, would function seamlessly without authentication errors. Additionally, I assumed that the automatic certificate renewal mechanism, introduced in Kubernetes 1.15 and later versions, would appropriately handle the expiration of certificates, including the kubelet certificate. The expectation was for a reliable and self-maintaining system, where certificate-related issues would be mitigated automatically.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Set up a Kubernetes cluster using version 1.26.1 with a specific configuration, including master nodes, worker nodes, and relevant components.
Introduce a scenario that intentionally triggers the authentication error in kubectl commands. This can be achieved by allowing a critical certificate, such as the kubelet certificate at /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt, to expire.


### Anything else we need to know?

title: Configmap can't exeed 8k in certain conditions
body:
### What happened?

Doing a healthcheck for php-fpm I disovered the kubernetes scheduler wasn't initialising the network correctly in certain conditions

How to reproduce:
- a big confirmap (around 6200 char all included, configmap name, name of the var and the content of them)
- the configmap needs to be used with `envFrom`
- a service needs to be running before the deployment exists (if you create the service after the deployment the issue don't occur)

When it's not working, the ip 127.0.0.1 don't answer correcly and the pod don't get the result of the command
```bash
❯ k exec deployments/php -c php -it -- sh
/var/www/html # cgi-fcgi -bind -connect 127.0.0.1:9000
/var/www/html # 
```


### What did you expect to happen?

the local network of a pod isn't answering correctly
```bash
❯ k exec deployments/php -c php -it -- sh
```
inside the pod on the ip 127.0.0.1 when it's working, we should see the result of cgi-fcgi
`cgi-fcgi -bind -connect 127.0.0.1:9000` the result should be:
```
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.11
Content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
```


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

First we create a service (it usually point into another pod with apache or nginx). But the pod is not needed to reproduce the issue. This is why the port 80 point on "no pod" but it dosen't matter in our case.
```yml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: service
spec:
  selector:
    app: php
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
```

this should not return you anything
```console
❯ k exec deployments/php -c php -it -- sh
```
inside the container
```console
/var/www/html # apk add fcgi
[...]
/var/www/html # cgi-fcgi -bind -connect 127.0.0.1:9000
/var/www/html # 
```
To "fix it" you need to delete de deployment and remove 1 char from the configmap:
now we rename the variable name ´var_nok:´ to ´var_ok:´
then delete de deployment and config map, wait 1-2 sec and deploy them again
```console
❯ k delete deployments.apps php && k delete configmaps config
```
now it works and this is the result:
```console
k exec deployments/php -c php -it -- sh 
```
inside the container
```console
/var/www/html # apk add fcgi
[...]
/var/www/html # cgi-fcgi -bind -connect 127.0.0.1:9000
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.11
Content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

/var/www/html # 
```

### Anything else we need to know?

1) The demo use php base image, you need to install fcgi first

2) It can be 1 to n variables, the only thing is that it needs to be the size of the confirmap that matters

3) You can also rename the name of the configmap to "crash" the network.
This fails too:
```yml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: configX
  namespace: default
data:
  var_ok: 
```

title: Pod with Finalizer: Can't delete the Pod
body:
### What happened?

We have a CronJob that creates Jobs which creates Pod which creates Containers. 

The Containers are state: terminated

The Pods are Status: Terminating

The Job is gone

The Pod has   finalizers:  - batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking  and I suspect that is why it won't delete.

I can't edit away the finalizer.

```
patch pod cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
The Pod "cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc" is invalid: spec: Forbidden: pod updates may not change fields other than `spec.containers[*].image`, `spec.initContainers[*].image`, `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds`, `spec.tolerations` (only additions to existing tolerations) or `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (allow it to be set to 1 if it was previously negative)
```

I can't delete the pod:

```
mhm@mhm:~$ k delete pods cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc --grace-period=0 --force
Warning: Immediate deletion does not wait for confirmation that the running resource has been terminated. The resource may continue to run on the cluster indefinitely.
pod "cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc" force deleted
```
```
mhm@mhm:~$ k delete pods cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc --wait=false
pod "cronjob-update-trigger-production-28194180-0-hgdzc" deleted
```

But the pod still exists.


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the Pods to get deleted, once the Job no longer exists. 

I expect the Pods to get deleted, when I try to delete them with --force

### Anything else we need to know?

I've found various docs on this:
- https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#job-tracking-with-finalizers
  - "The controller removes the finalizer only after the Pod has been accounted for in the Job status"
  - But what if the Job doesn't exist? 

> Note: When you use a podFailurePolicy, the job controller only matches Pods in the Failed phase. Pods with a deletion timestamp that are not in a terminal phase (Failed or Succeeded) are considered still terminating. This implies that terminating pods retain a [tracking finalizer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#job-tracking-with-finalizers) until they reach a terminal phase. Since Kubernetes 1.27, Kubelet transitions deleted pods to a terminal phase (see: [Pod Phase](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-phase)). This ensures that deleted pods have their finalizers removed by the Job controller.

These guys recommend patching the pod to remove finalizers, but that doesn't work as I showed above:

https://containersolutions.github.io/runbooks/posts/kubernetes/pod-stuck-in-terminating-state/#solution-a

I also found some stuff here: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/12/29/scalable-job-tracking-ga/#deprecation-notices

> In the 1.26 release, we deprecated the annotation batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking and the control plane will stop adding it in Kubernetes 1.27. Along with that change, we will remove the legacy Job tracking implementation. As a result, the Job controller will track all Jobs using finalizers and it will ignore Pods that don't have the aforementioned finalizer.

title: Image pull from private registry fails because of missing credentials
body:
### What happened?

When trying to pull a image from a private registry the request is executed without any kind of authorization.

The secret is manually created with
`kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=dc.json --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`

`dc.json` is a file like the following:
```json
{
    "auths": {
        "somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io": {
            "auth": "XYZ"
        }
    }
}
```
where XYZ is the base64 encoding of `:refresh_token` (there is no username as I want to dynamically get a token from a OAuth endpoint)

My pod is then specifying the `imagePullSecret` pointing to the `regcred` from above.

When creating the pod, after setting up a mitmproxy, I can see the following requests:
- HEAD to `https://somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/v2/whateverimage/manifests/latest` which correctly fails with a 401 and returns a `Www-Authenticate` header set to `Bearer realm="https://somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/oauth2/token",service="somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io",scope="repository:whateverimage:pull"`
- Then the request to the `/oauth2/token` endpoint is executed. The problem here is that it is executed as a GET (opposed to being a POST) and without the expected URLEncoded form including the refresh_token from the imagePullSecret.

Executing a `HTTPS_PROXY="127.0.0.1:8080" crictl pull --auth "XYZ"  somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io/whateverimage` gives me no issues and the image is pulled successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the kubelet and the container runtime to properly talk to each other, but I am either doing something wrong or there is a bug 😄 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create an Azure Container Registry (or any image registry that is capable of OAuth AuthN)
- Setup a mitmproxy to watch the outgoing requests
- `kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=dc.json --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` where `dc.json` is a file like the following:  
  ```json
  {
      "auths": {
          "somecontainerregistry.azurecr.io": {
              "auth": "XYZ"
          }
      }
  }
  ```  
  (and XYZ is the base64 encoding of `:refresh_token`)
- Create a Pod referencing the imagePullSecret from above
- Check in mitmproxy there are 2 requests, one of the two should be a HEAD to `/v2/whateverimage/manifests/latest` and the other should be a POST (not a GET as above)

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_


This in turn causes pod events to be missed for other controllers, for example, the replicaset controller does not see that all of the pods are ready as it never receives the corresponding events from the watch channel. When scaling down the deployment, some pods get stuck because the kubelet seems to miss their deletion, and so on.

It's amazing how satisfying a fast bisect is

The reproducer was starting watches with no resource version specified, which was always documented to pass through to storage:

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#resource-versions

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/980082/e4a9507e-23de-40b9-b422-f77ff2244964)

#115096 fixed a bug in the implementation of that to *actually* serve watch requests like that from etcd.

Critically, informers do use resource versions whenever possible when they start watches, so I would not expect the bugfix in  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115096 to impact controllers like replicaset controller.

closing since the change in list/watch requests getting routed to etcd was a correctness bugfix to match documented behavior, and informers either set resourceVersion (to be able to be handled by the watch cache) or were paginating (and were already not being handled by the watch cache)

/close

It's even more than that - they always set RV when watching - they may sometimes set RV unset for list requests, but they should always set RV for watch requests.
So that seems like some kine issue...

Yeah, something is definitely wrong with Kine, but the increase in load or traffic caused by this change in behavior seems to be the trigger. I'm still tracking that down, but I appreciate y'all pointing me at the source of the change in behavior, that's one less thing to try to pin down.

title: The e2e CI test for the Garbage collector in sig-api-machinery is reporting an error
body:
### What happened?

Kubernetes e2e suite: [It] [sig-api-machinery] Garbage collector should support orphan deletion of custom resources [sig-api-machinery]

As stated in https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/util/wait/poll.go#L84:
```
// Deprecated: This method does not return errors from context, use PollUntilContextTimeout.
// Note that the new method will no longer return ErrWaitTimeout and instead return errors
// defined by the context package. Will be removed in a future release.
func PollWithContext(ctx context.Context, interval, timeout time.Duration, condition ConditionWithContextFunc) error {
	return poll(ctx, false, poller(interval, timeout), condition)
}
```
When I replace PollWithContext with PollUntilContextTimeout in the test directory, the CI always returns the following error:
[Related links](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/121401/pull-kubernetes-e2e-ec2/1717584584415121408)
```
{ failed [FAILED] failed to ensure the dependent is not deleted: client rate limiter Wait returned an error: rate: Wait(n=1) would exceed context deadline
In [It] at: test/e2e/apimachinery/garbage_collector.go:1110 @ 10/26/23 17:14:08.526
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The testcase can pass consistently.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In the code where the error occurs, replace PollWithContext with PollUntilContextTimeout

title: CVE-2023-5044: Code injection via nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/permanent-redirect annotation
body:
### Issue Details
A security issue was identified in [ingress-nginx](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx) where the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/permanent-redirect annotation on an Ingress object (in the `networking.k8s.io` or `extensions` API group) can be used to inject arbitrary commands, and obtain the credentials of the ingress-nginx controller. In the default configuration, that credential has access to all secrets in the cluster.

This issue has been rated **High** ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:L](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:L)), and assigned **CVE-2023-5044**.

### Affected Components and Configurations

This bug affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running `kubectl get po -n ingress-nginx`.

If you are running the “chrooted” ingress-nginx controller introduced in v1.2.0 (gcr.io/k8s-staging-ingress-nginx/controller-chroot), command execution is possible but credential extraction is not, so the High severity does not apply.

Multi-tenant environments where non-admin users have permissions to create Ingress objects are most affected by this issue.

#### Affected Versions

- <v1.9.0

#### Versions allowing mitigation

- v1.9.0

### Mitigation

Ingress Administrators should set the --enable-annotation-validation flag to enforce restrictions on the contents of ingress-nginx annotation fields.

### Detection

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](mailto:security@kubernetes.io)

### Additional Details

See ingress-nginx Issue [#10572](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126817) for more details.

### Acknowledgements
This vulnerability was reported by Jan-Otto Kröpke (Cloudeteer GmbH)

Thank You,
CJ Cullen on behalf of the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

For all three these issues the exploitation is similar to what is described on this page: https://raesene.github.io/blog/2023/10/29/exploiting-CVE-2023-5044/
Only the approach to escape from the current nginx config context differs.

`enable-annotation-validation` does enable additional validations. Unfortunately, they are just regular expressions working in blacklist mode. This never gives 100% assurance that mitigation works. https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/main/internal/ingress/annotations/parser/validators.go#L62

There are some checks here: https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/main/internal/ingress/inspector/rules.go#L25 but they are easily bypassable.

As you can see here, configuration-snippet is not validated: https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/main/internal/ingress/annotations/snippet/main.go#L36 anyway.

> Many people are using the remediation suggested by @cjcullen in their k8s cluster. If it is not effective, can we work and update the description to mention controller.allowSnippetAnnotations: false instead ?

I have a lot of questions why these stories were closed at all, as the product is still affected and suggested mitigations are "mitigations" at best (even if they would work), but not fixes.

On the other hand, configuration snippet annotation is indeed now disabled by default, which is indeed the best way to tackle this particular finding. :)

We take the same path here as other projects, ingress-nginx, nginx, even kubernetes can be deployed in an insecure way. We are trying to provide security and user flexibility. The annotations validation is a small step in that direction. Disabling snippets is a way for an administrator to mitigate the issue altogether as you pointed out. Any time you allow users to run untrusted code it could result in security flaws. We are actively trying to brake out the security model for data plane and the control plane to help increase the security of the controller. If you have other suggesti9ns @pna-nca please join our community meetings and we can discuss them. If there are serious security concerns still please disclose them by emailing secuirty@kubernetes.io

> We are actively trying to brake out the security model for data plane and the control plane to help increase the security of the controller.

Good to hear!
My suggestion is to avoid closing security vulnerabilities without investing sufficient time into validating the provided mitigations. I understand it is usually not trivial and time consuming. Luckily, the community provided quite some doubts already to reconsider the previously made decision.

I would suggest pinpointing that for this particular finding the mitigations are the following:
- Keeping the (now default) setting `allowSnippetAnnotations: false`
- If the above is not possible, limiting and auditing the number of users which are allowed to use `configuration-snippet` annotation. OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies can do their job for this.

For vulnerability CVE-2023-5044 (`permanent-redirect`) the provided mitigation (`enable-annotation-validation`) will work, as basically only valid URL is expected.

Vulnerability CVE-2022-4886 (`ImplementationSpecific`) path is a really complicated beast. By definition user is allowed to use regular expressions there, which means "weird" symbols. However, as controller just inserts the provided setting into nginx config file, this might lead to config context escape. In order to avoid that one may just forbid `ImplementationSpecific` types via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno. However, this feature is way more used than even `configuration-snippet`. The provided mitigation in the closed finding is vague, `enable-annotation-validation` is not complete in this case as well, because dangerous symbols are [allowed](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/main/internal/ingress/annotations/parser/validators.go#L52). I would adjust validation on controller' side and allow less characters in regex.

> Any time you allow users to run untrusted code it could result in security flaws.

That is why we are relying on containerization. :) In this case, the controller provides functionality to adjust web server's configuration directly, without doing context-aware escape. It is similar to granting users a freedom of editing web page they are viewing: everything is fine, until there is an adversary (compromised user) which injects JavaScript to this page and benefit from others.

title: CVE-2022-4886: ingress-nginx path sanitization can be bypassed
body:
### Issue Details
A security issue was discovered in [ingress-nginx](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx) where a user that can create or update ingress objects can use directives to bypass the sanitization of the `spec.rules[].http.paths[].path` field of an Ingress object (in the `networking.k8s.io` or `extensions` API group) to obtain the credentials of the ingress-nginx controller. In the default configuration, that credential has access to all secrets in the cluster.

This issue has been rated **High** ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)), and assigned CVE-2022-4886.

### Affected Components and Configurations
This bug affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running `kubectl get po -n ingress-nginx`.

If you are running the “chrooted” ingress-nginx controller introduced in v1.2.0 (gcr.io/k8s-staging-ingress-nginx/controller-chroot), command execution is possible but credential extraction is not, so the High severity does not apply.

Multi-tenant environments where non-admin users have permissions to create Ingress objects are most affected by this issue.

#### Affected Versions

- <v1.8.0

#### Versions allowing mitigation

- v1.8.0

### Mitigation
Ingress objects contain a field called pathType that defines the proxy behavior. It can be Exact, Prefix and ImplementationSpecific.

When pathType is configured as Exact or Prefix, there is more strict validation, allowing only paths starting with "/" and containing only alphanumeric characters and "-", "_" and additional "/".

When this option is enabled, the validation happens in the Admission Webhook, denying creation of any Ingress containing invalid characters (unless pathType is ImplementationSpecific).

https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/user-guide/nginx-configuration/configmap/#strict-validate-path-type

Ingress Admins should enable this validation by default. If you still need to allow implementation specific paths due to the usage of features like Regex/rewrite on path, we recommend implementing countermeasures to allow just trusted users to consume this feature, as an example with OPA: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/examples/openpolicyagent/

### Detection
If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](mailto:security@kubernetes.io)

### Additional Details
See ingress-nginx Issue [#10570](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126815) for more details.

### Acknowledgements
This vulnerability was reported by Ginoah, working with the DEVCORE Internship Program.

Thank You,
CJ Cullen on behalf of the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

Hi @cjcullen I think you mis-typed your description.

> When pathType is configured as Exact or Prefix, there *is* more strict validation

should read as

> When pathType is configured as Exact or Prefix, there *should be a* more strict validation

This is important because although the English is not great, it is saying that the strict validation that there "should be" is enabled by setting the `strict-validate-path-type` option, it is not saying that the validation is already strict and the option does something else.
Can this CVE be mitigated for type `ImplementationSpecific` by disallowing to set the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex` annotation (using OPA)?

title: Kubernetes CronJob pods is not getting clean-up when Job is completed

title: When Pod fails to schedule during bind stage, PVC and PV are still bound, prevent pod reschedule to another node
body:
### What happened?

In my cluster, I have three nodes, each belonging to different availability zones: us-east-1a, us-east-1b, and us-east-1c. I have a StatefulSet resource with a replica count of 3, set podManagementPolicy as Parallel to allow creating pods in parallel. The StatefulSet resource uses volumeClaimTemplate to declare the use of persistent storage. To ensure that the three pods are scheduled in different zones, I've also configured the topologySpreadConstraints.

When kube-scheduler decides to schedule pod-A to node-1(assume pod in kube-scheduler's cache), kube-scheduler will add an annotation `volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node: node-1` on PVC to notify external provisioner to create PV and bound with PVC for pod-A.

The problem is sometimes pod-A scheduling fails at bind stage for some reason. kube-scheduler removes the assumed pod-A from cache, and adds it to the backoff queue for rescheduling, **but PV and PVC for pod-A remain bound to the node and won't be cleaned up.**

The next pod, pod-B, is then scheduled and happens to be assigned to the same node, without considering that the previous pod-A had already created a PVC and PV on that node. Pod-B successfully schedules on node-1. 

**When it's time to reschedule pod-A, it's unable to schedule to another node because pod-A's PVC is already bound to node-1. Furthermore, due to topologySpreadConstraints limits, pod-A cannot be scheduled to the same node (node-1) as pod-B**. As a result, pod-A remains in pending state forever. Even if I add new nodes to the cluster later, pod-A still won't be scheduled to other nodes. Currently, the only solution is to delete pod-A and PVC-A so that pod-A can be rescheduled to a different node.

Here is the StatefulSet definition.

title: [KCCM]: service update while node sync is processing might impact ingress
body:
### What happened?

The Kubernetes cloud controller manager uses resource watchers to sync load balancers, a Node/Service watcher. The Node watcher is slower by nature since any Node event will sync all service load balancers on the cluster. The service watcher is quicker since it only syncs the service load balancer which the event relates to. 

How slow a Node sync is will vary on the cluster, i.e: amount of Services of `type: LoadBalancer` and Nodes, but on big clusters with a lot of churn: the time to process one Node sync can be sufficiently slow to have the cache of Nodes go stale w.r.t the actual cluster state. The cache of Nodes is here the resource informer cache. When syncing Nodes the Node control loop will list all Nodes in its cache and then iterate over all Services and sync their load balancers in parallel, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L799-L818

If any Service experiences an update needing a load balancer sync, the Service controller will also list the Nodes in the informer cache, but retrieve a more up-to-date copy, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L438-L451. 

During upgrades or similar operations where a lot of Nodes get added/deleted: it's rather easy for the following to occur;

1. Node sync is processing, N load balancers are synced
2. NodeY is added
2. Service update triggers sync for load balancer X. It lists and adds NodeY to the load balancer set
3. Node sync processes load balancer Y and removes NodeY from the load balancer set 

This add + remove from the load balancer set might impact ingress SLOs for any application running on NodeY after its creation. 

/sig network
/cc @thockin @aojea 

### What did you expect to happen?

Any node added to the load balancer set which doesn't have a reason (i.e: [predicate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L996-L1016)) to be removed should not be removed from the load balancer's set of backend nodes.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Update a Service while an upgrade is on-going. Nodes risk being added/removed/added from the load balancer's set of backend nodes at sporadic moments. Alternatively, I have written a unit tests that exhibits the issue and while file a fix PR where this can be seen.  

### Anything else we need to know?

```
}

find $2 -type f | xargs sed -i '/generation: [0-9]\+/d'

#icdiff -r --no-bold --head=5000 --line-numbers --cols $(tput cols) $@

```

title: [kubelet-image-gc] minimum-image-ttl-duration not work,when kubelet restart.
body:
### What happened?

when kubelet restart,all images which notused cleaned.
but there is a flag in kubelet,`minimum-image-ttl-duration`,explain：Minimum age for an unused image before it is garbage collected.  Examples: '300ms', '10s' or '2h45m'.
i set `minimum-image-ttl-duration` to `20m0s`,it's means if a image not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet（if has disk pressure）.if kubelet not restart, it work,but if restart ther is a bug, `minimum-image-ttl-duration` not work,image will be clean，even if it's no enough  time.


### What did you expect to happen?

`minimum-image-ttl-duration` work, image even if not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1）make node trigger disk pressure.
2）pull some image which not used by pod
3）restart kubelet
4）image cleaned by kubelet after around 10s

### Anything else we need to know?

i see the source code, and maybe there is a bug.

in [detectImages](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L261-L262) func,well detect image and update firstdetect time for every image.
```go
	// New image, set it as detected now.
		if _, ok := im.imageRecords[image.ID]; !ok {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID is new", "imageID", image.ID)
			im.imageRecords[image.ID] = &imageRecord{
				firstDetected: detectTime,
			}
		}
```
and in  [freeSpace](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L394C1-L397) func,well check images livetime by firstDetected.
```go
		if freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID's age is less than the policy's minAge, not eligible for garbage collection", "imageID", image.id, "age", freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected), "minAge", im.policy.MinAge)
			continue
		}
```
if kubelet running normal,it work,because there is a [Start](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L190-L204) func.
```go
func (im *realImageGCManager) Start() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	go wait.Until(func() {
		// Initial detection make detected time "unknown" in the past.
		var ts time.Time
		if im.initialized {
			ts = time.Now()
		}
                // in first time,ts is zero. 
               // in first time,ts is zero.
		_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)
		if err != nil {
			klog.InfoS("Failed to monitor images", "err", err)
		} else {
			im.initialized = true
		}
	}, 5*time.Minute, wait.NeverStop)
//...

```
in this line,`_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)`,in first time,ts is zero. so image's firstDetected time is zero,and in freeSpace
`reeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge` this check is always false,so image will be cleaned.


maybe we can change to `im.detectImages(time.now())`,can fix this bug.

title: CVE-2023-3893: Insufficient input sanitization on kubernetes-csi-proxy leads to privilege escalation
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/av:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) - **HIGH** (8.8)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where a user that can create pods on Windows nodes running kubernetes-csi-proxy may be able to escalate to admin privileges on those nodes. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if they include Windows nodes running kubernetes-csi-proxy.

### Am I vulnerable?

Any kubernetes environment with Windows nodes that are running kubernetes-csi-proxy is impacted.  This is a common default configuration on Windows nodes.  Run `kubectl get nodes -l kubernetes.io/os=windows` to see if any Windows nodes are in use.

#### Affected Versions

- kubernetes-csi-proxy <= v2.0.0-alpha.0
- kubernetes-csi-proxy <= v1.1.2

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

The provided patch fully mitigates the vulnerability and has no known side effects.  Full mitigation for this class of issues requires patches applied for CVE-2023-3676, CVE-2023-3955, and CVE-2023-3893.

Outside of applying the provided patch, there are no known mitigations to this vulnerability.

#### Fixed Versions

- kubernetes-csi-proxy master - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/306
- kubernetes-csi-proxy v2.0.0-alpha.1 - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/307
- kubernetes-csi-proxy v1.1.3 - fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy/pull/306

To upgrade: cordon the node, stop the associated Windows service, replace the csi-proxy.exe binary, restart the associated Windows service, and un-cordon the node.  See the installation docs for more details: https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-proxy#installation

If a Windows host process daemon set is used to run kubernetes-csi-proxy such as https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-driver-smb/blob/master/charts/latest/csi-driver-smb/templates/csi-proxy-windows.yaml, simply upgrade the image to a fixed version such as ghcr.io/kubernetes-sigs/sig-windows/csi-proxy:v1.1.3

### Detection

Kubernetes audit logs can be used to detect if this vulnerability is being exploited. Pod create events with embedded powershell commands are a strong indication of exploitation.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was discovered by James Sturtevant @jsturtevant and Mark Rossetti @marosset during the process of fixing CVE-2023-3676 (that original CVE was reported by Tomer Peled @tomerpeled92)

title: k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel immediately executes condition twice
body:
### What happened?

While trying to update https://github.com/flatcar/flatcar-linux-update-operator/blob/7a1b0ff2769af91e8ff2bae82fc93f2f5baf0b0c/pkg/agent/agent.go#L328 to use latest version of `wait` package and to migrate away from deprecated `PollImmediateUntil`, function, our tests fail as it seems new `PollUntilContextCancel` function immediately executes given condition twice, which is not mentioned anywhere.

Result of executed test specified below:
```console
$ go test . -v
=== RUN   Test_test
=== PAUSE Test_test
=== CONT  Test_test
=== RUN   Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Unexpected early timestamp
=== RUN   Test_test/PollImmediateUntil
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:02 +0000 UTC m=+2.000000001
--- FAIL: Test_test (3.00s)
    --- FAIL: Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel (0.00s)
    --- PASS: Test_test/PollImmediateUntil (3.00s)
FAIL
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Since `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollImmediateUntil` has been deprecated and it recommends using `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel`, I expected it to have the equivalent semantics to allow easy migration from deprecated functions, as no changelog or documentation mentions new semantics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Playground: https://go.dev/play/p/qQBnWM4nufF

Local:
1. `go mod init foo && go get k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait`
2. Create `main_test.go` file with the following content:
```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

const (
	testTimeout           = 3 * time.Second
	callsExpectedInterval = 2 * time.Second
)

func Test_test(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), testTimeout)
	t.Cleanup(cancel)

	t.Run("PollUntilContextCancel", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollUntilContextCancel(ctx, callsExpectedInterval, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil })
	})

	t.Run("PollImmediateUntil", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollImmediateUntil(callsExpectedInterval, func() (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil }, ctx.Done())
	})
}

func testIntervals(t *testing.T) func() {
	t.Helper()

	timestamps := make(chan time.Time, 1)

	timestamps <- time.Now().Add(-1 * 2 * callsExpectedInterval)

	return func() {
		t.Helper()

		t.Logf("Executed at %s", time.Now())

		if timestamp := <-timestamps; timestamp.After(time.Now().Add(-1 * callsExpectedInterval / 2)) {
			t.Fatalf("Unexpected early timestamp")
		}

		timestamps <- time.Now()
	}
}
```
3. Run as `go test . -v`.

title: Resource(CPU, memory, device, topology) managers don't consider restartable init containers
body:
### What happened?

Resource(CPU, memory, topology) managers don't consider restartable init containers.

- [x] CPU manager: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119447
- [x] Memory manager: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120715
- [x] Device manager: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120461
- [ ] Topology manager:

---

When cpu-manager-policy is static and you create a guaranteed pod with a restartable init container,
a restartable init container shares its static CPUs with a regular container.


### What did you expect to happen?

A restartable init container should not share its CPU requirement with the regular containers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
$ cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init-1
    image: ubuntu
    command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - |
      grep Cpus_allowed_list /proc/self/status | cut -f2
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared
      mountPath: /tmp/shared
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 8
        memory: 100Mi
  - name: restartable-init-2
    image: ubuntu
    command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - |
      grep Cpus_allowed_list /proc/self/status | cut -f2
      sleep 300s
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared
      mountPath: /tmp/shared
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 4
        memory: 200Mi
    restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: regular-3
    image: ubuntu
    command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - |
      grep Cpus_allowed_list /proc/self/status | cut -f2
      sleep 300s
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 4
        memory: 300Mi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared
      mountPath: /tmp/shared
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
  volumes:
  - name: shared
    emptyDir: {}
  restartPolicy: Never
EOF
pod/test created
...
$ kubectl logs test -c init-1
0-3,6-9
$ kubectl logs test -c restartable-init-2
0-1,6-7  # init container and restartalbe init container can share the CPUs, as "init-1" is already terminated and will not restart.
$ kubectl logs test -c regular-3         
0-1,6-7  # restartable init container and regular container should not share the CPUs, as they should run together.
```

title: suggested code change to enable 'go vet' to report printf mistakes in the source
body:
### What happened?

(This isn't a bug report, but I couldn't find a more appropriate category.)

The k8s Go source code contains a number of places where printf-like functions are called with arguments of the wrong type. Ordinarily, the 'go vet' tool would point out such mistakes, but unfortunately it's not smart enough to figure out that loggingT.printfDepth behaves like printf, because it obscures the call delegation with extra computation. However, the trivial patch below would make the connection obvious:

```
 func (l *loggingT) printfDepth(s severity.Severity, logger *logr.Logger, filter LogFilter, depth int, format string, args ...interface{}) {
+       if false {
+               _ = fmt.Sprintf(format, args...) // cause vet to treat this function like printf
+       }
```

and cause vet to discover a number of mistakes, such as these:

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Currently, the downward API tests flake on Windows with a failure to allocate memory when starting the ``agnhost`` binary used in these tests. The tests are spawning pods with a memory limit of 64MB, which is a bit on the low side for a Windows Pod, even if it's a nanoserver-based image.
